newsitem.title: UK: British doctors take anti-boxing debate to cinema.
newsitem.headline: British doctors take anti-boxing debate to cinema.

text.p: British doctors are taking their campaign to ban boxing to the cinema with the release of a 60-second film that highlights the dangers to the brain from persistent heavy punching.
The doctors' main professional body, the British Medical Association (BMA), launched the film on Wednesday. It will show in around 100 cinemas around Britain over the next two months.

The black and white film has a boxing commentary over what seems to be a close-up in silhouette of a game of conkers -- a game played by British children with horse chestnuts suspended from string. The aim is to smash the opponent's conker.
In the film, the conkers smash into each other, but when one falls to the ground, it turns out to be a brain.
The film ends with the words: "Where's the sport in boxing?"
Sandy Macara, chairman of the BMA council, told a news conference that boxing was "not a sport but a brutal, outdated activity".
The BMA has counted at least nine deaths from boxing in amateur or professional bouts around the world since 1985.
Most recently, in October 1995, a 25-year-old Scottish bantamweight, James Murray, was knocked out and, after medical attention was delayed by a crowd riot, died 36 hours later.
"No one now disputes that boxing can lead to both acute and chronic brain damage, and every year that passes sees more young boxers dying or suffering irreversible damage," Macara said.
But former world featherweight champion Barry McGuigan did dispute it. "There is no shred of evidence that there is insidious damage to boxers," he told BBC radio.
Current British featherweight champion Colin McMillan -- who was allowed into the news conference on condition he did not try to speak -- was also irritated by the BMA campaign.
"I do find it strange that they continue to try to get boxing banned. There are a lot of sports more dangerous -- rugby, car racing, American football," he said.
He doubted the campaign would have much effect but said if it were successful it would only push boxing underground and lead to unsafe, unregulated bouts.
"Rather than the BMA trying to attack it, it would be more beneficial if it came inside and helped make it safer," he said.
